title: How do you implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot: add the `grpc-spring-boot-starter` dependency and the protobuf Maven/Gradle plugin, define your `.proto` file, run code generation, annotate the server implementation with `@GrpcService` (extends the generated `ImplBase`), and inject a client stub with `@GrpcClient("service-name")`: and how does service discovery and health checking integrate (gRPC health checking protocol, Kubernetes gRPC probes, Eureka/Consul)?
shortTitle: How do you implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot, and how do service discovery and health checking integrate?
keyPoints: Add grpc-spring-boot-starter plus the protobuf Maven or Gradle plugin to generate stubs and server base classes from the .proto file.
Annotate the server implementation with @GrpcService and extend the generated ImplBase so the starter registers it on the embedded gRPC server automatically.
Inject a client stub with @GrpcClient naming the service, and configure the address and negotiation type in application.yml.
Service discovery resolves the logical service name to live instances via Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes headless-service DNS for client-side load balancing.
The gRPC Health Checking Protocol exposes a built-in Health service with Check and Watch methods returning SERVING or NOT_SERVING.
From Kubernetes 1.24 onward, native gRPC probes call the Health service directly for readiness and liveness without a custom script.
Prefer client-side load balancing with a headless service for gRPC, because a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection through an L4 load balancer pins all calls to one pod.

s1_definition.oneliner: @GrpcService registers the server and @GrpcClient injects the stub, a registry or Kubernetes DNS resolves the service name, and the standard gRPC health protocol lets Kubernetes probe readiness natively.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`grpc-spring-boot-starter`** – Auto-configures a Netty-based gRPC server and client management in a Spring Boot application.
- **`@GrpcService`** – Annotation that registers a gRPC server implementation class, which extends the generated `ImplBase`, with the embedded server.
- **`@GrpcClient("name")`** – Annotation that injects a generated client stub into a Spring bean, resolving the service name from `application.yml`.
- **Service discovery** – Resolves the logical service name through Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes headless-service DNS so the client finds live instances.
- **gRPC Health Checking Protocol** – A built-in `grpc.health.v1.Health` service with `Check` and `Watch` methods that Kubernetes can probe natively from version 1.24.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India wiring up a new department. The grpc-spring-boot-starter is the office manager who automatically sets up the phone line and the reception desk the moment you hire a department, so you just annotate the department as open for business with @GrpcService. When another department needs to call it, it simply asks for it by name with @GrpcClient, and the building directory (Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes DNS) tells it which rooms currently have staff. The health check is the daily roll call: a supervisor periodically asks each department "are you ready to serve?" and routes customers only to the ones that say yes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot you add the grpc-spring-boot-starter and the protobuf build plugin with the gRPC Java plugin, define the proto file, and let the build generate the stubs and server base classes. The starter autoconfigures an embedded gRPC server on its own port and scans for beans annotated with @GrpcService. The server class simply extends the generated ImplBase and carries @GrpcService, and it is registered automatically. To consume it from another service, inject a stub into any bean with @GrpcClient naming the service, and a matching entry in application.yml gives the address and negotiation type.

Service discovery is where the client stops using a hard-coded address and instead resolves the logical service name to live instances. With Eureka or Consul the client resolves something like discovery:///transfer-service to the registered instances. In Kubernetes, a headless service DNS returns all pod IPs so the client sees every instance and can client-side load balance across them with a round-robin policy. That client-side load balancing matters specifically for gRPC, because a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection through a plain layer-four load balancer would pin every call to one pod.

Health checking uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol, which is a built-in Health service with a Check method that returns SERVING or NOT_SERVING and a Watch for streaming updates. The starter can expose this automatically, and from Kubernetes 1.24 onward there is a native gRPC probe, so readiness and liveness probes just say grpc on the port and Kubernetes calls the Health service directly instead of needing a custom script.

In banking work at National Bank of India the transfer service ran as several pods, and this wiring meant other services called it simply by name, Kubernetes routed traffic only to ready pods, and load spread evenly across them. The senior detail to always add is to tie the reported health to real readiness: keep the status NOT_SERVING until the database connection pool is warmed up and only then flip it to SERVING, so Kubernetes never routes a transfer to a pod that would immediately fail.

Remember one sentence: @GrpcService registers the server and @GrpcClient injects the stub, while a headless DNS and the gRPC health protocol let Kubernetes discover and probe pods natively.
